name: Kabocha squash
tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, roasted beside anything
why_now: Kabocha is the squash that comes after the thin-skinned early ones — dense, dry, and sweeter than butternut, with a flavor somewhere near chestnut. It's picked now and actually improves after a few weeks on the counter, which makes it the first thing in the year you can buy in October and cook in November.
how_to_choose: Dark green, dull rather than shiny — shine means it was picked early
A pale orange patch on one side is fine; that's where it sat on the ground
buy_this_much: 1 large, about 3 lbs. That's two trays of roasted wedges — most of a week of bowls and tacos.
price_note: Usually sold by the pound. Cheaper at Asian and Mexican markets than at most supermarkets.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted wedges
flavor_paths.description: Skin on, oil, salt, 425°F until the edges char. The default.

flavor_paths.name: With muhammara
flavor_paths.description: Hot wedges, a spoonful of the jar, arugula on top.

flavor_paths.name: With yogurt
flavor_paths.description: Salted yogurt underneath, pomegranate on top. Sweet, sour, cold, hot.

weekday_uses: Roasted wedges over rice with muhammara
Cubed in tacos with black beans and cotija
Next to salmon on the same sheet pan
Cold, straight from the fridge, with salt
weekend_use: A tray of dark-roasted wedges on the table beside the whole fish, for anyone who wants something warm next to the salad.
storage: Whole, somewhere cool and dry for up to two months — it gets sweeter over the first few weeks. Once cut, wrap it and refrigerate; use within five days.
one_thing_to_learn: Kabocha is drier than other squash, which is why it roasts so well: there's less water to steam off before the sugars can brown. That's also why it can taste chalky if undercooked. Roast it until a knife slides in with no resistance at all, then give it five more minutes.
market_question: How long ago was this picked?
